subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science - Biology: Infection and Response
subtitle: Revision pack covering infectious disease, pathogen spread, body defences, immune response, vaccination, antibiotics, hygiene and investigation skills.
description: Reading passages for KS3 biology covering infectious disease, pathogen transmission, body defences, vaccination, antibiotics, public health and scientific data interpretation.

data.sourcePassage: An infectious disease is caused by a pathogen and can be passed from one organism to another. Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and some protists. Bacteria are tiny living cells and some can reproduce quickly or release toxins that cause symptoms. Viruses are not cells. They must enter living body cells and use the cells to make more viruses. Fungi can grow on or in the body, and some spread by spores or by contact with infected skin, towels or floors. Not all microorganisms are harmful. Many bacteria and fungi are useful, such as gut bacteria, yeast used in bread making and decomposers in ecosystems.

questions.question: What is an infectious disease?
questions.modelAnswer: A disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one organism to another.

questions.question: Which pathogen type is not made of cells?
questions.modelAnswer: Viruses are not cells.

questions.question: Why can bacteria cause symptoms?
questions.modelAnswer: Some bacteria reproduce quickly or release toxins that affect body cells.

questions.question: Explain why it is wrong to say all microorganisms are pathogens.
questions.modelAnswer: Many microorganisms do not cause disease and some are useful, such as gut bacteria, yeast and decomposers.

questions.question: Which example is a fungal infection from the source?
questions.modelAnswer: Athlete's foot is a fungal infection.

data.sourcePassage: Pathogens spread by transmission. A chain of infection starts with an infected person or source, then the pathogen leaves the body, travels by a route, enters a new host and may cause infection. Routes include droplets from coughs and sneezes, direct contact, contaminated food or water, contaminated surfaces, breaks in the skin and vectors such as insects. Prevention works by breaking one or more links in the chain. Covering coughs reduces droplets leaving the body. Handwashing removes pathogens from hands. Cleaning surfaces reduces transfer from desks and handles. Cooking food thoroughly kills many bacteria or stops them reaching the digestive system alive.

questions.question: Name two transmission routes from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include droplets, direct contact, contaminated food or water, contaminated surfaces, breaks in skin and vectors.

questions.question: What does handwashing mainly remove from hands?
questions.modelAnswer: Handwashing removes pathogens from hands.

questions.question: How does covering a cough break the chain of infection?
questions.modelAnswer: It reduces droplets containing pathogens leaving the body and reaching other people or surfaces.

questions.question: Why can touching the mouth after touching a contaminated surface lead to infection?
questions.modelAnswer: Pathogens on the hand can enter the body through the mouth and may then survive and multiply.

questions.question: Explain why prevention measures reduce risk rather than making infection impossible.
questions.modelAnswer: They break some transmission routes and lower pathogen transfer, but they do not remove every pathogen or control every exposure.

data.sourcePassage: The body has first lines of defence that try to stop pathogens entering. Skin is a physical barrier. If skin is cut, blood clotting and a scab help seal the break while the skin heals. Mucus in the nose and airways traps dust and pathogens, and cilia move mucus out of the airways. Stomach acid kills many swallowed pathogens. If pathogens get past these barriers, white blood cells respond. Some engulf pathogens. Others make antibodies that fit specific antigens on pathogens. The word specific is important: an antibody made for one antigen may not fit a different antigen.

Stomach acid kills many swallowed pathogens. If pathogens get past these barriers, white blood cells respond. Some engulf pathogens. Others make antibodies that fit specific antigens on pathogens. The word specific is important: an antibody made for one antigen may not fit a different antigen.

questions.question: Why is skin described as a physical barrier?
questions.modelAnswer: It forms a layer that blocks many pathogens from entering body tissues.

questions.question: Which defence moves mucus out of the airways?
questions.modelAnswer: Cilia move mucus out of the airways.

questions.question: How does a scab help prevent infection?
questions.modelAnswer: It seals a break in the skin while new skin grows underneath, reducing pathogen entry.

questions.question: What do some white blood cells make to target pathogens?
questions.modelAnswer: They make antibodies that fit specific antigens on pathogens.

questions.question: Why might an antibody for one pathogen not protect well against another pathogen?
questions.modelAnswer: Antibodies are specific, so they fit particular antigens. A different pathogen may have different antigens.

data.sourcePassage: A vaccine trains the immune system before a person meets the real pathogen. It may contain a harmless form, inactive version or small part of a pathogen. White blood cells respond and memory cells may remain. If the real pathogen enters later, the immune response can be faster and stronger. Vaccines are mainly used for prevention and do not usually cure an infection that is already happening. Antibiotics are different. They treat bacterial infections by killing bacteria or stopping them reproducing, but they do not kill viruses. Antibiotic resistance happens when bacteria survive an antibiotic and reproduce, making resistant bacteria more common.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a vaccine?
questions.modelAnswer: A vaccine trains the immune system before exposure to the real pathogen.

questions.question: What type of infection do antibiotics treat?
questions.modelAnswer: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections.

questions.question: How do memory cells help after vaccination?
questions.modelAnswer: They help the immune system respond faster and more strongly if the same pathogen enters later.

questions.question: Why do antibiotics not kill viruses?
questions.modelAnswer: Viruses do not have the same bacterial cell processes that antibiotics target.

questions.question: Explain why unnecessary antibiotic use can make resistance more common.
questions.modelAnswer: Antibiotics kill or stop susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant bacteria to survive and reproduce.

data.sourceTitle: Evidence from Handwashing and Vaccination Data
data.targetTitle: Evidence from Handwashing and Vaccination Data
data.sourcePassage: Scientists use evidence to test ideas about infection and prevention. In a handwashing investigation, the independent variable might be handwashing time, while the dependent variable might be the amount of UV gel left on hands or the number of colonies on a sealed agar plate. Control variables could include soap type, water temperature, amount of gel, incubation time or sampling method. Repeats help check reliability and identify anomalies. Data can suggest patterns, such as fewer colonies after longer washing or fewer disease cases when vaccination uptake is higher. However, correlation does not automatically prove cause because other factors may also affect the results.

questions.question: In a handwashing investigation, what could the independent variable be?
questions.modelAnswer: Handwashing time could be the independent variable.

questions.question: Which is a possible control variable?
questions.modelAnswer: Soap type could be kept the same as a control variable.

questions.question: Why are repeats useful in an investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: Repeats help check whether results are consistent, improve reliability and identify anomalies.

questions.question: What pattern might longer handwashing show in the source investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: Longer handwashing reduced the amount of UV gel left on hands, suggesting more model pathogen was removed.

questions.question: Why should a student be careful when claiming that vaccination was the only reason cases fell?
questions.modelAnswer: The data may show correlation, but hygiene, travel, reporting, population size or other factors could also affect cases.
